name: Battle of Ain Jalut
info: On 3 September 1260 the Bahri Mamluks of Egypt under Sultan Qutuz defeated a Mongol force of the Ilkhanate under Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut in the Jezreel Valley, and the Mamluks then took Damascus and Aleppo.

facts.place: Near the spring of Ain Jalut at the northwestern foot of Mount Gilboa, in southeastern Galilee in the Jezreel Valley, about 15 km north-northwest of Baysan
facts.sides: The Bahri Mamluks of Egypt under Sultan Qutuz, with Baybars commanding the vanguard; the Ilkhanate's army under Kitbuqa, between 10,000 and 12,000 men by one estimate, with Georgian, Armenian and Ayyubid contingents
facts.outcome: The Mongol force was driven back and Kitbuqa died with most of the army that remained in the region. The Mamluks took Damascus five days later and Aleppo within a month.

t: Hulegu left Syria with the bulk of his army after the death of Möngke Khan, leaving Kitbuqa a far smaller force when the Mamluks advanced from Cairo.
The Mamluks used a smaller force under Baybars to draw the Mongols into the highlands, where the rest of their army waited in hiding.
Hulegu could not avenge the defeat, in part because of his quarrel with Berke Khan of the Golden Horde, and the Mongols never returned to Syria.
dyk: Qutuz killed Hulegu's envoys and displayed their heads on Bab Zuweila, one of the gates of Cairo, before he marched. He was himself assassinated on the way back to Cairo after the victory, in a conspiracy led by Baybars, who became sultan.
ev: Hulegu's army captures and sacks Baghdad, and the Abbasid Caliphate is destroyed
Hulegu's envoys demand Qutuz's surrender, and Qutuz kills them and displays their heads at Cairo
Hulegu withdraws with the bulk of his army, leaving Kitbuqa about one tumen west of the Euphrates
Qutuz leaves Cairo on 26 July, and Baybars takes Gaza
The Mamluk and Mongol armies meet at Ain Jalut on 3 September, and Kitbuqa is killed
Damascus falls to the Mamluks five days later and Aleppo within a month; Qutuz is assassinated and Baybars becomes sultan
A Mongol force of two tumens takes Aleppo in December and massacres many Muslims, but withdraws after a fortnight

sections.background:
Möngke Khan became Great Khan in 1251 and set out to carry out his grandfather Genghis Khan's plan for a world empire. He chose his brother Hulegu to subdue the nations of the west. Assembling the army took five years, and Hulegu was ready to begin only in 1256. Möngke ordered good treatment for those who yielded without resistance and destruction for the rest. Other countries in the Mongols' path submitted and contributed forces, so that by the time the army reached Baghdad it included Cilician Armenians and some Frankish troops from the Principality of Antioch.

The Assassins in Persia fell, the 500-year-old Abbasid Caliphate of Baghdad was destroyed in 1258, and the Ayyubid dynasty in Damascus fell as well. Hulegu's plan was then to move south through the Kingdom of Jerusalem towards the Mamluk Sultanate, the major Islamic power.

In 1260 Hulegu sent envoys to Qutuz in Cairo with a letter demanding his surrender. Qutuz killed the envoys and displayed their heads on Bab Zuweila. Möngke Khan was slain in battle against the Southern Song, and Hulegu returned to Mongolia with the bulk of his army to attend the kurultai in accordance with Mongol custom. He left approximately 10,000 troops west of the Euphrates under Kitbuqa. Most of the Mamluks were Kipchaks, and the Golden Horde's supply of Kipchaks replenished the Mamluk armies.
sections.forces:
Kitbuqa was a Naiman Nestorian Christian general. The army left to him was one tumen, nominally 10,000 men but usually fewer. The Mamluk chronicler al-Yunini gives the Mongol army with its vassals as 100,000 men, a figure that is likely an exaggeration. Kitbuqa's strength is put at between 10,000 and 12,000 soldiers, including Georgian and Lesser Armenian battalions (about 500 Cilician Armenians), the contingents of two Ayyubid princes, al-Ashraf Musa and al-Said Hasan, and local levies that had served the Syrian Ayyubids.

Qutuz assembled a large army at Cairo and left on 26 July 1260 for al-Salihiyya. It was made up of Egyptian troops, the Syrian battalions of al-Nasir Yusuf, Shahraziriyya Kurds, Arabs and Turcomans. Al-Maqrizi claims that the amirs at al-Salihiyya declined to attack the Mongols until Qutuz overcame their opposition with a powerful speech. He put Baybars at the head of the vanguard, and Baybars took Gaza, a Mongol outpost, before its commander Baydara could receive orders from Kitbuqa. The route north ran through Frankish territory. The rulers of Acre, after lengthy discussion, stayed neutral, let Qutuz pass and supplied his army on the plain of Acre.

Kitbuqa chose to stand at Ain Jalut, a perennial spring at the northwestern foot of Mount Gilboa, where the Wadi Jalut gave water for horses, the valley offered pasture and good ground for cavalry, and the slopes of Gilboa secured a flank. The evidence strongly indicates that the Mongols arrived first and took up their positions.
sections.course:
The Mongols advanced first. The Mamluks knew the ground, and Qutuz hid the bulk of his force in the highlands and meant to bait the Mongols with a smaller force under Baybars. Both armies fought for many hours, with Baybars using hit-and-run tactics to provoke the Mongols while keeping the bulk of his troops intact. When the Mongols made another heavy assault, Baybars and his men feigned a final retreat to draw them into the highlands, where the rest of the Mamluk force was concealed among the trees. Kitbuqa, already provoked by the repeated flight of Baybars's men, advanced with all his troops. The Mamluks then emerged, shot arrows and attacked with their cavalry, and the Mongols were surrounded on all sides. Timothy May hypothesises that a key moment was the defection of the Mongols' Syrian allies.

The Mongols fought hard to break out. Qutuz watched with his private legion, and when he saw the left wing of the Mamluk army almost destroyed by the Mongol attack he threw away his helmet so that his men could recognise him and cried out three times to God for victory. He then rushed towards the weakened side, shouting wa islamah, followed by his own unit. The Mongols were pushed back and fled towards Beisan, followed by Qutuz's forces. They reorganised and returned to make a successful counterattack, but the battle shifted towards the Mamluks, who now held the advantage of ground and morale, and some of the Mongols were forced to retreat. Kitbuqa, with almost all the rest of the Mongol army that had remained in the region, perished.
sections.aftermath:
Hulegu ordered the execution of the last Ayyubid emir of Aleppo and Damascus, an-Nasir Yusuf, and his brother, who were in captivity, when he heard of the defeat. The Mamluks captured Damascus five days after Ain Jalut and Aleppo within a month. On the way back to Cairo Qutuz was assassinated by several emirs in a conspiracy led by Baybars, who became the new sultan. Local Ayyubid emirs sworn to the Mamluk sultanate then defeated another Mongol force of 6,000 at Homs, which ended the first Mongol expedition into Syria.

Hulegu could not bring his full power against the Mamluks. Berke Khan of the Golden Horde, who had converted to Islam, was horrified at the destruction of the Abbasid caliph. Rashid al-Din quotes him as writing that Hulegu had sacked all the cities of the Muslims and caused the death of the caliph. The Mamluks learned through spies that Berke was a Muslim and no friend of his cousin, and cultivated ties with him. In December 1260 Hulegu sent two tumens to attack the Mamluks in Aleppo. They massacred a large number of Muslims in retaliation for the death of Kitbuqa but, after a fortnight, made no further progress and withdrew. Hulegu returned to his lands by 1262 and massed his armies, but Berke's raids lured him north, and he suffered a severe defeat in 1263 in an invasion north of the Caucasus, the first open war among the Mongols. He died in 1265 and was succeeded by his son Abaqa.
sections.sources:
The battle is known from Mamluk and Persian writers. Al-Yunini and al-Maqrizi are the sources for the Mamluk side, and Rashid al-Din Hamadani for Berke's message. The large number of sources in vastly different languages has led Mongol historians to focus on limited aspects of the empire. Studies of the battle include those by Amitai-Preiss, Halperin and John Masson Smith, whose 1984 paper is titled "Ayn Jalut: Mamluk Success or Mongol Failure?".

Several points are uncertain or disputed. Strengths are known only as estimates: al-Yunini's 100,000 for the Mongols is likely an exaggeration. That Baybars laid out the overall strategy is only said to be so, because he had spent time in the region as a fugitive. The sources differ on where Kitbuqa was camped before the battle: Rashid al-Din has him at Ba'labakk and al-Yunini on the Biqa plain. May's suggestion about the defection of Syrian allies is a hypothesis. Ahmad Yousef al-Hassan holds that Mamluk hand cannon were used, which would make it the earliest known use; David Ayalon, Iqtidar Alam Khan, Joseph Needham, Tonio Andrade and Gabor Ágoston contradict this, and Khan believes cannon reached Mamluk Egypt only in the 1370s. A recent study argues that a short climate anomaly after the Samalas eruption may have contributed to a Mongol withdrawal.
sections.legacy:
The battle has been described by numerous academic and popular historians as epochal: the first time a Mongol advance met a major defeat and a permanent halt. It was the first of two defeats the Mongols suffered in trying to invade Egypt and the Levant, the other being the Battle of Marj al-Saffar in 1303. Beside Ain Jalut the Mongols were beaten at the second Battle of Homs, Elbistan and Marj al-Saffar; in five battles with the Mamluks they won only at Wadi al-Khaznadar, and they never returned to Syria. Baybars and his successors went on to capture the last of the Crusader states in the Holy Land by 1291.

The defeat also coincided with the end of the unified Mongol empire, since the war between Hulegu and Berke was the first open war among the Mongols. In later memory the name has been taken up in modern politics: one of the three original brigades of the Palestine Liberation Army was named Ain Jalut, and in July 1970 Yasser Arafat referred to the battle, saying that the Mongols who had swept away the Abbasid caliphate were defeated at Ain Jalut, in the same region where he said his people were then fighting the Zionists.

summary: On 3 September 1260 the Bahri Mamluks of Egypt under Qutuz met a Mongol force under Kitbuqa at Ain Jalut and drove it back, killing Kitbuqa. The Mamluks then took Damascus and Aleppo, and the Mongols never returned to Syria.
notes: The article contradicts itself on Möngke: its opening says he was slain shortly after Hulegu's envoys were killed, but the Aftermath says Berke protested the attack on Baghdad without knowing Möngke had died. I followed the Background and Prelude for Hulegu's departure and said no more.
The article spells names variously (Kitbuqa, Kitbugha, Ketbugha; Baybars, Baibars). I used Kitbuqa and Baybars throughout.
No Mamluk strength is given. The present-day country of the site is not named in the article, so the facts say only southeastern Galilee, Jezreel Valley.
The article says Hulegu's sole attempt after the battle was the two-tumen attack on Aleppo in December 1260, yet also says he massed armies in 1262; I told both as given.
The turn of the battle (Qutuz's charge, the Mongol retreat to Beisan and counterattack) has no times in the article.
Left out: the article's claim that Kitbuqa 'committed a grave mistake' (a judgement), the Frankish attitudes to the Mongols in detail, and the Mongol vassal levels beyond what is stated.
The Arafat statement is paraphrased and attributed; no comment on present governments is made.
